[Gathered by ApprovalReady from official websites on 2026-10-11; a summary, not the source's wording] How to get: Register a company (Pty Ltd) with ASIC (Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC); director IDs are issued by Australian Business Registry Services (ABRS)).
A company is a separate legal entity, so you register it with ASIC to get an Australian Company Number (ACN) before it can trade. Every director must have a director ID before being appointed, and the company pays an annual review fee every year it stays registered.
Timeframe: About 15 minutes online once you have everything ready; confirmation usually within 2 business days if documents are complete and the fee is paid.
Cost: A$636 to register a proprietary company (from 1 July 2026), then a A$342 annual review fee each year. Director IDs are free.
Before you start: Make sure a company suits you: sole traders, partnerships and trusts do not register with ASIC as companies. A company has extra legal duties and ongoing costs.
Before you start: Every director must apply for their own director ID before they are appointed. It is free, done through ABRS, and you keep it for life even if you change companies.
Before you start: To apply for a director ID online you need a Digital ID such as myID with at least Standard identity strength, plus your ATO-held residential address and details from two verification documents (for example a notice of assessment). Giving your TFN is optional but speeds things up.
Before you start: Choose a name that shows legal status (for example 'Example Pty Ltd') and check it on ASIC's name availability search, or let ASIC use your ACN as the name.
Before you start: Decide your state or territory of registration, registered office address and principal place of business.
Before you start: Decide your internal rules: the replaceable rules in the Corporations Act 2001, your own constitution, or a mix.
Before you start: Work out the share structure and members. For each member you need name and address and written consent; for each director and secretary you need full name (including former names), home address, date and place of birth, and signed written consent to act, which you must keep.
Before you start: If the company will trade under a name other than its exact company name, it needs a separate business name registration.
Step 1: Each director gets a director ID. Every proposed director applies for their own director ID through ABRS before the company is registered. Online is fastest: sign in with myID (Standard or Strong), answer the identity questions and submit; your ID appears on screen. If you cannot get a myID with at least Standard strength, ABRS has other ways to apply depending on where you live. (time: Immediate online; cost: Free)
Step 2: Choose and check the company name. Check the name on ASIC's name availability search. You can optionally reserve a name for up to 2 months using ASIC Form 410 if you are not ready to register. (cost: Name reservation fee applies (amount not confirmed); form: Form 410 Application for reservation of a name)
Step 3: Prepare company details and consents. Prepare the registered office and principal place of business addresses, your rules (replaceable rules or constitution), share classes and numbers, member details and written consents, and each officeholder's details and signed consent to act.
Step 4: Register through the Business Registration Service. Apply to register the company (proprietary limited, public, or special purpose) in the Business Registration Service and pay the fee. You can add the company's ABN, GST, PAYG withholding and a business name in the same application. Some cases, such as hiding a residential address or an unlimited company, need a paper form or business service provider instead. (time: About 15 minutes; confirmation usually within 2 business days; cost: A$636 (proprietary company, from 1 July 2026); form: Business Registration Service)
Step 5: Receive your ACN, certificate and corporate key. The Business Registration Service emails the ACN and certificate of registration. ASIC posts the corporate key to the registered office; you need it to use ASIC's company officeholder portal. Show the company name wherever the company trades publicly, and put the name and ACN on required documents.
Step 6: Do the annual review every year. ASIC sends an annual statement after your review date (usually the registration anniversary). Check and update the company details, pass a solvency resolution, and pay the annual review fee. Keep company records and the share register up to date throughout the year. (time: Each year; late fees apply if not paid within 2 months of the review date; cost: A$342 (proprietary company, from 1 July 2026))
Fee: Register a proprietary company: A$636.00 (From 1 July 2026 (up from A$611))
Fee: Annual review fee, proprietary company: A$342.00 (From 1 July 2026 (up from A$329))
Fee: Director ID: A$0.00 (Free to apply)
Contact: ASIC: 1300 300 630, https://www.asic.gov.au/about-asic/contact-us
Contact: Australian Business Registry Services (director IDs): 13 62 50, https://www.abrs.gov.au/director-identification-number
Contact: business.gov.au contact centre: 13 28 46, https://business.gov.au/
Watch out: Becoming a director without a director ID is an offence (60 penalty units). Applying for more than one director ID, or misrepresenting yours, can mean up to 1 year in prison.
Watch out: From 1 July 2027 companies must give their directors' IDs to ASIC.
Watch out: Late fees apply if the annual review fee is not paid within 2 months after the review date.
Watch out: Directors have legal duties under the Corporations Act 2001; understand them before you agree to act.
Watch out: A company name does not cover other trading names. Register a business name for any other name you trade under.
Watch out: Moving from sole trader to company means a new ABN for the company and transferring any business name.

[Gathered by ApprovalReady from official websites on 2026-10-11; a summary, not the source's wording] How to get: Apply for an Australian Business Number (ABN) (Australian Business Register (ABR), administered by the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) as part of Australian Business Registry Services).
An ABN is the 11-digit number that identifies your business to government and other businesses. It is free, and you need one to invoice properly, avoid having tax withheld from payments you receive, claim GST credits and get an .au domain name. You can only get one if you are carrying on, or starting, an enterprise.
Timeframe: Usually issued immediately at the end of the online application. If you get a reference number instead, the ABR aims to review it within 20 business days.
Cost: Free. Applying for an ABN through the Australian Government costs nothing; private websites that charge a fee are not required.
Before you start: Check you pass the entitlement test: you must be carrying on or starting an enterprise in Australia (or be a Corporations Act company). Signs of a business include significant commercial activity, an intention to make a profit shown by a business plan, repeated and systematic activity run in a business-like way, and relevant skill.
Before you start: You are not entitled to an ABN for work you do as an employee (including apprentices, trade assistants and labourers, even if it is called contracting), or for a hobby. An employer should not make an ABN a condition of employment.
Before you start: If you have not started trading yet, you should already have taken some start-up steps, such as advertising, setting up a website or social media, getting licences or insurance, leasing premises or equipment, giving quotes or applying for finance.
Before you start: Choose your business structure first (sole trader, partnership, company or trust). It changes what the application asks and which other registrations you need, and changing structure later can mean a new ABN.
Before you start: Have your tax file number (TFN) ready, plus the TFNs of any associates such as partners, directors or trustees. Being identifiable from your TFN speeds the application up.
Before you start: Have ready: the date you need the ABN from (no more than six months in the future), your entity's legal name, business address, postal address, email and phone, your main business activity, the physical locations you operate from, and your ACN if you are a company.
Before you start: Email addresses must be 5 to 200 characters with no spaces and must not begin with support@, sales@ or info@.
Before you start: If you use a registered tax or BAS agent, have their agent number so they can be an authorised contact.
Step 1: Confirm you are entitled to an ABN. Read the ABR entitlement guidance and make sure your activity is an enterprise, not employment or a hobby. Keep evidence (business plan, quotes, licences, insurance, lease, adviser correspondence) because the ABR can review your entitlement at any time and ask you to prove you started, or took steps to start, your business from the date on your application. Applying without entitlement can lead to prosecution.
Step 2: Gather the information the application asks for. Collect your TFN and associates' TFNs, the ABN start date, legal name, business and postal addresses, contact details, main business activity, business locations, any previous ABN, your ACN (companies), and your tax or BAS agent number if you use one. You can save a part-finished application, but missing details will likely delay your ABN.
Step 3: Apply online through the Business Registration Service. Use the Australian Government Business Registration Service at register.business.gov.au. In the same application you can also apply for a business name, GST, an Australian company, PAYG withholding, fringe benefits tax, luxury car tax, fuel tax credits and wine equalisation tax, so you only enter your details once. (time: Most applications are finished in one sitting; cost: Free; form: Business Registration Service)
Step 4: Read the outcome at the end of the form. If approved you get your 11-digit ABN on screen straight away; save or print the confirmation. If you get a reference number, the ABR needs to check your details and aims to review within 20 business days; check ABN Lookup and expect a confirmation letter within 14 days of approval. If refused, you get a refusal number and a letter within 14 days explaining why and your review rights. (time: Immediate, or up to 20 business days if reviewed)
Step 5: Keep your ABN details up to date. Update your ABN details within 28 days of becoming aware of a change. Cancel your ABN if you close or sell the business, stop operating in Australia, or change structure (for example sole trader to company, sole trader to partnership, or partnership to company), and apply for a new one for the new structure. (time: Within 28 days of a change)
Fee: ABN application: A$0.00 (Free through the Australian Business Register / Business Registration Service)

Before you start: Work out whether you are an introducer: AICIS says anyone who imports or manufactures industrial chemicals for commercial purposes must register, including businesses, sole traders and individuals, and including people importing products that contain industrial chemicals.
Before you start: Add up the value of the industrial chemicals you imported or manufactured in the previous financial year (for 2026-27 registration, 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026). Before you start: Have your business details ready so you can enrol in AICIS Business Services, the online portal used for registration, renewals and declarations.
Before you start: Be ready to categorise every chemical you introduce. Each chemical (including each ingredient in a mixture) must fall into one of five categories: listed, exempted, reported, assessed, or commercial evaluation authorisation. AICIS publishes free decision tools to help.
Before you start: Set up a record-keeping system from day one. AICIS says you must keep records for 5 years, even after you stop introducing the chemical, and provide them within 20 working days if asked (stated for assessed introductions).
Before you start: If you will not introduce industrial chemicals after 31 August, tell AICIS through the 'advise of non-renewal' option in AICIS Business Services rather than just letting registration lapse.
Step 1: Work out your registration level. Use the AICIS registration calculator. Your level is based on the total value of industrial chemicals you imported or manufactured in the previous financial year (1 July to 30 June). The calculator also shows your fee and levy. Level 1 is A$0 to A$49,999 and level 8 is A$15,000,000 or more. (time: Before you register)
Step 2: Enrol in AICIS Business Services. New users create an account in AICIS Business Services, the AICIS online portal. Follow the AICIS guidance on creating an account. Step 3: Register or renew for the registration year. In AICIS Business Services, open the Registration section and select the registration year (2026-27). AICIS says its decision tools are general guidance only and a completed decision tool is not enough on its own to meet your record-keeping obligations. Keep records for 5 years. Medicines, vitamins and supplements, and medical devices must generally be entered in the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG) before you can lawfully supply them in Australia. An Australian sponsor applies to the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA), pays application fees and annual charges, and takes legal responsibility for the product. Importing for your own personal use is a separate, limited scheme and cannot be used for resale.
Timeframe: Medical devices: the TGA makes its preliminary assessment decision within 20 business days of a paid application, longer if selected for audit. Listed (AUST L) medicines are validated electronically and listed on submission; registered medicines take much longer.
Cost: From 1 July 2026: a listed medicine (AUST L) costs A$1,063 to apply plus A$1,566 a year; a Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring) medical device costs A$651 to apply plus A$121 a year; Class IIa/IIb devices A$1,244 plus A$1,305 a year; Class III A$1,603 plus A$1,662 a year. Audits and registered medicines cost much more.
Before you start: Confirm your product is a therapeutic good at all. Some products are regulated as foods or cosmetics instead, and some goods are excluded or exempt (Schedules 5, 5A and 7 of the Therapeutic Goods Regulations 1990 list product exemptions).
Before you start: Search the ARTG. If the product is already on it, you may be able to buy from the existing sponsor and sell as a retailer instead of becoming a sponsor yourself, though commercial agreements may prevent this.
Before you start: Decide who will be the sponsor. The sponsor is the person or company that supplies the goods in Australia and is legally responsible for them. If you import directly from the manufacturer and are the first point of supply, you need TGA approval as sponsor.
Before you start: For medical devices, get a written agreement with your manufacturer so you can obtain technical information quickly. You must answer TGA information requests within set timeframes and allow inspections.
Before you start: Confirm the manufacturer meets requirements: overseas medicine sites need GMP clearance, and device manufacturers need conformity assessment evidence (for example an overseas certificate the TGA accepts) or a TGA conformity assessment certificate.
Before you start: For listed (AUST L) supplements, check every ingredient is a permitted ingredient and every claim is a permitted indication, and hold evidence for your claims before you list.
Before you start: Budget for ongoing annual charges and post-market duties: adverse event reporting, recalls, advertising code compliance, and keeping records (devices: up to 10 years or the device's lifetime).
Step 1: Create a TGA Business Services (TBS) account and register your organisation. Sponsors and manufacturers must register their details with the TGA before seeking approval. TGA Business Services (also called eBS) is the primary application portal for applications and ongoing compliance. Keep your contact details current.
Step 2: Medical devices: classify the device and submit manufacturer evidence. Work out the device class and category. Certain Class I, Class 1 IVD and export-only devices need only a manufacturer's declaration of conformity with the application. All others need manufacturer evidence (such as conformity assessment certificates) submitted in TBS and accepted by the TGA before you draft the inclusion application. One accepted piece of evidence can support multiple applications.
Step 3: Medical devices: apply for ARTG inclusion and pay. Lodge the inclusion application in TBS. You receive an invoice after submission and the TGA does not review the application until it is paid. Application fees are non-refundable. The TGA aims to make a preliminary assessment decision within 20 business days. Outcomes are approved, selected for audit (extra time and audit fees), or refused. (time: Preliminary decision within 20 business days of payment; cost: A$651 (Class I) to A$1,603 (Class III) application fee; audit fees from A$4,926 if selected)
Step 4: Listed medicines (most vitamins, minerals, herbal supplements): list through the electronic listing facility. Listed complementary medicines can contain only permitted low-risk ingredients and make permitted indications. You apply through the electronic listing facility in TGA eBusiness Services; the application must pass electronic validation, and you certify that the product meets all legal requirements. The TGA does not evaluate the claims before listing, but runs random and targeted compliance reviews. Each listed product gets an AUST L number that must appear on the label. (time: Listed once the application validates and is submitted; cost: A$1,063 application fee and A$1,566 annual charge (from 1 July 2026))
Step 5: Registered medicines: apply for evaluation. Higher-risk products (registered complementary medicines, over-the-counter medicines and prescription medicines) are evaluated before they are entered on the ARTG. Fees depend on the application level (for example OTC N1 to N5, registered complementary RCM1 to RCM5). (cost: From A$2,077 + A$5,133 (OTC N1) upward)
Step 6: Pay annual charges and claim the annual charge exemption if eligible. Annual charges are levied in July each year for every ARTG entry that existed at any time in the financial year. Products entered on or after 1 July 2015 can get an annual charge exemption until they generate turnover. Self-declarations must reach the TGA between 1 July and 22 July each year; late declarations before 15 September cost extra. To avoid next year's charge, ask for cancellation by 30 June. (time: Declarations 1 to 22 July each year; cost: See fees)
Step 7: Meet post-market obligations. Report adverse events, support recalls, follow the Therapeutic Goods Advertising Code, keep information on the ARTG current (lodge variations when things change), and for devices notify the TGA within 60 days if manufacturer evidence is suspended, revoked or lapses. Fee: Registered complementary or OTC medicine annual charge: A$2,061.00 (From 1 July 2026)
Fee: OTC medicine N1 application + evaluation: A$7,210.00 (A$2,077 application + A$5,133 evaluation, from 1 July 2026)

Fee: Medical device Class I (other) annual charge: A$121.00 (Class I sterile or measuring: A$879)
Fee: Medical device Class IIa or IIb application: A$1,244.00 (Annual charge A$1,305)
Fee: Medical device Class III application: A$1,603.00 (Annual charge A$1,662 (AIMD annual charge also A$1,662))
Fee: IVD medical device application (all classes): A$1,244.00 (Annual charge A$948 (except Class 4 in-house))

Watch out: Annual charges apply for every financial year an ARTG entry exists, even if you sold nothing, unless you lodge the exemption declaration between 1 and 22 July. Cancel unwanted entries by 30 June.

Before you start: Get test reports against the relevant Australian standard. For Level 2 you need a compliance folder; for Level 3 you need a certificate of conformity issued by a recognised external certification scheme (RECS) certifier or Energy Safe Victoria, listed on the national register.

Step 5: Mark the equipment with the RCM. As responsible supplier, you authorise the Regulatory Compliance Mark. For Level 1 you may do so once you have evidence of compliance; for Level 2 and 3, once the equipment is registered. Contact: WorkSafe Queensland: 1300 362 128, https://www.worksafe.qld.gov.au/contact

Watch out: Registering Level 2 or 3 equipment as Level 1 is not permitted and could result in penalties.
Watch out: You must not sell in-scope equipment without the RCM.
Watch out: The responsible supplier must be a legally identifiable Australian or New Zealand entity with an ABN or NZ IRD number, so an overseas manufacturer cannot register in your place.

[Gathered by ApprovalReady from official websites on 2026-10-11; a summary, not the source's wording] How to get: Import declaration and customs clearance (Australian Border Force) (Australian Border Force (Department of Home Affairs)).
Goods you bring into Australia must be cleared from customs control. If a consignment is worth more than A$1,000 you (or a licensed customs broker) must lodge a full import declaration (N10) and pay duty, GST and charges before the goods are released. Consignments of A$1,000 or less that arrive by air or sea are usually cleared on a self-assessed clearance (SAC) declaration, generally with no duty or GST, except alcohol and tobacco.
Timeframe: No fixed lodgement deadline is published for an N10. The cargo reporter reports cargo before arrival, and goods are not released until the declaration is cleared and duty, GST and charges are paid. Allow 30 days if you want a free written Tariff Advice before you buy.
Cost: Over A$1,000: an Import Processing Charge of A$50 (electronic, under A$10,000) or A$152 (electronic, A$10,000 or more), plus a DAFF biosecurity full import declaration charge of A$48 (air) or A$71 (sea), plus customs duty at the rate in the tariff, plus 10% GST on the value of the taxable importation. Broker fees, freight, storage and handling are extra and are not set by government.
Before you start: Work out the value of the whole consignment in Australian dollars. Over A$1,000 means a full import declaration (N10) and payment of duty, GST and the Import Processing Charge. A$1,000 or less arriving by air or sea can usually go on a self-assessed clearance (SAC). International mail uses form B374 instead of a SAC.
Before you start: Tobacco, tobacco products and alcoholic beverages attract duty and taxes at any value, even under A$1,000.
Before you start: Check whether the goods are prohibited or restricted and need a permit from another agency (for example biosecurity, therapeutic goods, chemicals, vehicles). If a permit is needed you must use an N10 or a long format SAC, not a cargo report SAC, and give proof of the permission to the ABF.
Before you start: Decide who lodges. The ABF encourages first-time or infrequent importers to use a licensed customs broker. You can self-lodge electronically only if you are registered in the Integrated Cargo System (ICS) with a Gatekeeper digital certificate, or you can lodge a paper form B650 at an ABF counter (higher charge).
Before you start: Get the tariff classification right. Classifications and duty rates are in Schedule 3 of the Working Tariff on the ABF website. If you are unsure, apply for a free Tariff Advice (form B102) before you order. It covers one good from one manufacturer and takes about 30 days.
Before you start: Check whether a free trade agreement (FTA) can lower your duty. Australia has FTAs with, among others, Japan (JAEPA), China (ChAFTA), Korea, the USA, the UK, the UAE, India and ASEAN countries. You must hold valid origin evidence (such as a certificate of origin or an origin declaration in the format the FTA requires) when you make the claim.
Before you start: Check whether a Tariff Concession Order (TCO) covers your goods. A TCO is a duty concession for goods with no substitutable Australian-made equivalent. Your goods must fall in the tariff classification and precisely match the TCO description.
Before you start: Have ready: the supplier's commercial invoice, the bill of lading (sea) or air waybill (air), packing list, any permits, origin evidence for FTA claims, and your ABN.
Step 1: Classify the goods and estimate duty and GST. Find the 8-digit tariff classification and statistical code in Schedule 3 of the Working Tariff. Check Schedule 4 for concessional items and the FTA schedules (for example Schedule 11 for Japan, Schedule 12 for China, Schedule 15 for the UK) for the preferential rate. GST is 10% of the value of the taxable importation, which is the customs value plus duty plus international transport and insurance (plus wine tax where it applies). Luxury car tax and wine equalisation tax (29%) can also apply. (time: Same day if the classification is clear)
Step 2: Get a binding Tariff Advice if the classification is unclear (optional). A Tariff Advice is an advance ruling on how specific goods will be classified, for intended imports of new goods. Lodge form B102 'Application for Advance Ruling (Tariff)' (print both sides) or lodge through TAPIN if you or your broker has access, then email the application and supporting documents to tariffclassification@abf.gov.au within 5 days. Give detailed information about the goods; the ABF cannot classify on insufficient information. Once issued you must follow it when importing those goods. (time: Service standard is 30 days; longer in busy periods; cost: Free from the ABF (a broker may charge to prepare it); form: B102 Application for Advance Ruling (Tariff))
Step 3: Arrange origin evidence before shipping if you will claim an FTA rate. Ask the supplier for the origin document the FTA requires before the goods ship. For example, under the Japan agreement (JAEPA) goods must be supported by a certificate of origin from an authorised body or an origin certification document completed by the importer, exporter or producer, valid for one year and for a single consignment. Under ChAFTA a declaration of origin can only replace a certificate of origin if the goods are covered by a current Origin Advance Ruling. Without valid origin evidence the claim can be refused and duty recovered with penalties. (time: Before shipment; cost: Certificates of origin are issued by authorised bodies, which set their own charges)
Step 4: Work out the customs value in Australian dollars. The customs value is usually the transaction value: the price you actually paid or will pay. Include overseas packing costs and any inland freight and insurance you paid before the goods left the place of export; exclude international freight and insurance to Australia. Adjust for commissions and royalties where required. Convert foreign currency at the rate on the day of export published by the ABF. If buyer and seller are related, the transaction value can be used only if the relationship did not affect the price.
Step 5: Lodge the import declaration (N10) or SAC. Electronic: lodge the N10 through the Integrated Cargo System yourself (if registered) or through a licensed customs broker. Paper: lodge form B650 (sea or air cargo) in person at an ABF counter with the bill of lading or air waybill, commercial invoices, proof of identity, and any permits. If the ABF flags your car you must give evidence; if that is not enough it will direct sampling and testing at the border at your cost, and asbestos parts are seized.
Timeframe: No fixed timeframe. Sort it out in Japan before shipping; a border hold for sampling and testing adds days to weeks of storage and delay.
Cost: No government fee. You pay for any parts replacement, technical evidence, sampling by an independent competent person, NATA-accredited testing, and storage while held.
Before you start: The ban applies to every vehicle regardless of type, age, value or country of origin, and to temporary imports. Japan banning asbestos does not mean a Japanese car is free of it; aftermarket parts are a common source.
Before you start: List the high-risk parts the ABF names: brake pads and shoes, clutch linings, gaskets (cylinder head, extractors, exhaust), seals (fuel tank, mastic, windows), bonnet liners, heater and air conditioner housings, fibrous washers, sound deadening, firewalls, heat shields, wiring wrap, body seam sealers, bituminous coatings and insulation.
Before you start: Decide your assurance route before shipping: technical evidence from the manufacturer that OEM parts are asbestos-free, records of replacing at-risk parts with documented asbestos-free parts, or an accredited test report that clearly links to this specific car and the parts tested.
Before you start: A seller's, supplier's or mechanic's informal statement is not enough evidence. 'Asbestos-free' labels under overseas standards may still allow low levels that are illegal here.
Before you start: Keep every record (work orders, parts invoices, test reports) and make sure they name the VIN or chassis number. The ABF can ask for them at any time.
Step 1: Assess the car's risk. Consider age, make, model, maintenance history and any aftermarket parts. Older cars and cars with replaced brakes, clutches or gaskets are higher risk. Ask your exporter or the selling dealer for service history. (time: Before you buy)
Step 2: Remove or test suspect parts in Japan. The ABF prefers testing or removing suspect parts before shipment, and notes that replacing them may be cheaper than sampling and testing. Keep work records and evidence of the make, model and composition of replacement parts. Overseas sampling and testing must meet Australian laboratory reporting requirements. (time: Before shipping)
Step 3: Make an honest declaration. Only make a 'no asbestos' declaration if you are certain, covering OEM and aftermarket parts and naturally contaminated materials. Your customs broker will ask about asbestos when lodging the import declaration.
Step 4: Respond if the ABF flags the car. If the ABF considers the car at risk, you (or your broker) must give sufficient assurance with documents. If the evidence is not enough, the ABF directs sampling and testing at the border and supervises it while the car is under customs control. (time: Depends on how fast you supply evidence)
Step 5: Arrange sampling and NATA-accredited testing if directed. You must engage a qualified, independent competent person to identify and sample suspect parts; the ABF does not take samples or remove asbestos. Analysis in Australia must be by a NATA-accredited laboratory. Storage costs while waiting are yours whether or not asbestos is found. (time: Days to weeks; cost: You pay sampling, testing and storage)
Step 6: Deal with any positive result. Goods found to contain asbestos are seized and forfeited for disposal. Asbestos parts must be removed under ABF control before the car can be released, and you may face penalties.

Contact: Asbestos Safety and Eradication Agency: 1300 326 148, enquiries@asbestossafety.gov.au, https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au

Watch out: Enthusiast car shows do not count as 'display', so you cannot get a permit to import an asbestos-containing car you plan to drive or show.
Watch out: Aftermarket brake pads, clutch kits and gaskets bought cheaply overseas are a common cause of detections.
